column4: The rhetorical question أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ directly answers the man's supposition that no one saw him: the obstructer is himself seen by Allah.
After the man supposed he would never return, بَلَىٰ إِنَّ رَبَّهُۥ كَانَ بِهِۦ بَصِيرًا overturns his supposition with the Lord's continuous sight, closely matching 90:7's structure.
إِنَّهُۥ ظَنَّ أَن لَّن يَحُورَ states the complacent man's false supposition; 84:15 answers it with the Lord who had always seen him, as 90:7 answers a false supposition about being unseen.
إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِٱلْمِرْصَادِ places the Lord at a watch post, directly realizing the section's mountaintop lookout and denying any unobserved deed.
Allah says He created the human, knows the soul's whisper, and is nearer than the jugular; creation, hidden thought, and intimate observation meet in one ayah.
The two receivers seated at right and left stage the watchers whose recording presence 50:18 brings to the man's speech.
No word is uttered without a ready رَقِيبٌ beside it; this directly joins 90:6's speech to the watcher hidden in the root of رَقَبَةٍ.
At the Fire, hearing, eyes, and skins testify against their owners; the given eye becomes a witness against the person who assumed he was unseen.
The skins explain that Allah, who makes everything speak, made them speak; the Creator of bodily perception can turn the body into testimony.
وَلَٰكِن ظَنَنتُمْ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَعْلَمُ names the very delusion behind 90:7: they supposed Allah did not know much of what they did.
This ayah says that their supposition about their Lord ruined them, completing the consequence of the unseen-observer delusion named in 41:22.
أَمْ يَحْسَبُونَ أَنَّا لَا نَسْمَعُ asks whether they suppose secret speech is unheard, then says the messengers beside them write it; it is the auditory counterpart of 90:7.
Allah knows خَآئِنَةَ ٱلْأَعْيُنِ and what breasts hide, making even the eye's covert betrayal visible to the watcher.
They hide from people but cannot hide from Allah, who is with them while they scheme at night; this directly exposes the empty space imagined by “no one saw.”
Whether speech is concealed or voiced, Allah knows what is within breasts; both the secret word and its inward source remain observed.
أَلَا يَعْلَمُ مَنْ خَلَقَ asks whether the One who created could fail to know, answering the section's question whether the maker of the eye could fail to see.
No affair, recitation, or deed is entered without Allah being witness as it begins, and not even an atom escapes Him.
Every secret council has Allah with it, however its members count themselves, and He will tell them their deeds; supposed privacy becomes witnessed account.
هُوَ مَعَكُمْ أَيْنَ مَا كُنتُمْ and His sight of deeds place every human location within the observing presence that 90:7 denies.
Nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah, a direct universal denial of the imagined unseen deed.
The Prophet is told not to suppose Allah unaware of what wrongdoers do; the repeated verb of supposition is corrected by delayed but exact observation.
People fold their breasts and cover themselves to hide, yet Allah knows both what they conceal and disclose; bodily concealment cannot produce an unwatched place.
Secret and public speech, hiding by night, and moving by day are equal before Allah, systematically closing every route by which the man might imagine himself unseen.
The keys of the unseen, every fallen leaf, and every grain in darkness are known and recorded, extending the watching image to what no created eye detects.
إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا names Allah as رَقِيب over people, the divine watcher latent in the section's ر ق ب word family.
Jesus contrasts his finite witnessing while among his people with Allah as ٱلرَّقِيبَ over them after his departure, clarifying the difference between human and divine surveillance.
وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ رَّقِيبًا gives the section's watcher-root its unrestricted divine scope.
وَلِتُصْنَعَ عَلَىٰ عَيْنِى uses “My eye” for Allah's protective oversight of Moses, exactly matching the dictionary's guarding sense of عَيْن.
فَإِنَّكَ بِأَعْيُنِنَا places the Prophet under divine eyes while he waits patiently, another direct Quranic realization of the protective-eye idiom.
Noah is commanded to build the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا; protective observation and divinely supplied knowledge accompany an act humans could not secure alone.
The repeated command to make the ark بِأَعْيُنِنَا وَوَحْيِنَا again binds the watching eye to revelation and rescue.
The ark runs بِأَعْيُنِنَا as recompense for the one denied, turning divine eyes into sustained guardianship through danger.
Allah reassures Moses and Aaron, إِنَّنِى مَعَكُمَآ أَسْمَعُ وَأَرَىٰ; hearing and seeing are protective presence before the tyrant.
The Lord يَرَىٰكَ حِينَ تَقُومُ, presenting divine sight of the Prophet's otherwise private rising.
وَتَقَلُّبَكَ فِى ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ continues 26:218's gaze into the Prophet's movements among those prostrating.
The close إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ completes the protective seeing scene with hearing and knowledge.
وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَٰفِظِينَ places guardians over people, filling the supposed absence of an observer.
كِرَامًا كَٰتِبِينَ identifies the guardians of 82:10 as honored recorders.
يَعْلَمُونَ مَا تَفْعَلُونَ gives the recorders exact knowledge of deeds, the consequence denied by 90:7.
إِن كُلُّ نَفْسٍ لَّمَّا عَلَيْهَا حَافِظٌ states that every soul has a guardian over it, a compact answer to the imagined vacant watch post.
The book omits neither small nor great and people find their deeds present; exhaustive recording makes the once-hidden act visible at judgment.
Each person's record is fastened to his neck and brought out as an open book, joining bodily neck imagery to an inescapable account.
The person is told to read his own book and is sufficient as his own accountant; observation finally returns as self-reading.
On the day of exposure, لَا تَخْفَىٰ مِنكُمْ خَافِيَةٌ states that no hidden thing belonging to a person remains hidden.
The left-handed speaker says وَلَمْ أَدْرِ مَا حِسَابِيَهْ, turning the section's د ر ي verb inward when the once-unseen account is handed to him.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good يَرَهُۥ; the doer himself ultimately sees the deed he might have thought no observer saw.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil يَرَهُۥ, completing the two-sided return of every deed to sight.
بَلِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِۦ بَصِيرَةٌ makes the human a witness against himself, even before the bodily testimony developed elsewhere.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify about what their owners used to do, extending the watching function beyond the two eyes.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned; the body supplies the witness the person imagined absent.
“Work,” then Allah, His messenger, and the believers will see the work; the command makes action explicitly answerable to multiple witnesses.
ٱعْمَلُوا۟ مَا شِئْتُمْ is immediately bounded by إِنَّهُۥ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ, turning apparent freedom from observers into a warning of exact sight.
Moses' sister sees him from a distance while his captors do not perceive her; a hidden watcher gathers news over the child already placed under Allah's eye.
Moses' sister walks after him and he is returned so his mother's eye may be comforted; this supplies the human watching and protective outcome surrounding 20:39's divine eye.
Moses is restored to his mother so her eye may be comforted and she may know Allah's promise is true, completing 28:11's distant watch.
Men on the Heights recognize every group by their marks; elevated lookout, visible signs, and identification of persons converge in a single scene.
When the watchers' eyes are turned toward the Fire's people, they beg not to be placed with wrongdoers; the lofty gaze reaches the threatened fire.
The people of the Heights call men they recognize by their marks, continuing the section's watch-post and visible-person senses.
The Fire itself رَأَتْهُم مِّن مَّكَانٍۭ بَعِيدٍ and they hear its rage; the expected gaze reverses, making the distant fire the watcher of its targets.
إِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ كَانَتْ مِرْصَادًا makes Hell an ambush or watch post, joining the lookout image directly to the fire disclosed by the section's questions.
The Knower of the unseen discloses His unseen to no one except a chosen messenger, sharply marking what a human cannot know until God informs him.
Allah sends guards before and behind the chosen messenger, joining communicated knowledge to an encircling watch.
The guarded disclosure establishes that the messages were delivered and that Allah encompasses and counts all things.
The jinn find heaven filled with powerful guards and flames, staging a defended observation post against would-be gatherers of hidden news.
Those who sat in listening stations now find a flame lying in wait, combining spying for news, a lookout seat, and fiery ambush.
The rebellious devils cannot listen to the highest assembly and are pelted from every side, making illicit news-gathering the object of vigilant defense.
They are driven away and assigned lasting punishment, the consequence of breaching the guarded listening scene.
The one who snatches a fragment of hearing is pursued by a piercing flame, a concise spy-and-hunter reversal.
The heaven is guarded from every expelled devil, supplying a cosmic instance of the section's guarding watcher.
Whoever steals a hearing is followed by a clear flame, again making the covert collector of news into visible prey.
Lamps adorn the nearest heaven and become missiles against devils, so distant visible lights also enforce the guarded boundary.
Reachable game tests who fears Allah unseen; the hunter believes the quarry exposed, while his own hidden restraint is what Allah tests and knows.
Moses says إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًا after perceiving a fire; it is the exact Quranic use of the section's dictionary sense of ء ن س for seeing or sensing something distant.
Moses again says إِنِّىٓ ءَانَسْتُ نَارًا and expects news or a burning brand, joining perception, distant information, and fire.
Moses perceives a fire from the mountain's side and hopes for news or an ember; the ء ن س sense, remote sign, lookout height, and fire all meet.
هَلْ تُحِسُّ مِنْهُم مِّنْ أَحَدٍ أَوْ تَسْمَعُ asks whether even one of the destroyed peoples can be sensed or heard, closely matching the idiom in which no eye means no person.
مَا زَاغَ ٱلْبَصَرُ وَمَا طَغَىٰ presents sight that neither swerves nor exceeds its limit, a precise boundary for the seeing faculty.
The seer beholds some of his Lord's greatest signs, joining disciplined vision in 53:17 to signs that truly must be seen.
The messenger is seen on the clear horizon, a visible person at a distance that closely realizes the dictionary's “man's sign is his visible form.”
Pharaoh's body is preserved so that he may be an ءَايَةً for those after him; a man's visible body literally becomes a sign.
The earth contains ءَايَٰتٌ for the certain, presenting signs as perceptible marks distributed before the observer.
وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَفَلَا تُبْصِرُونَ turns the gaze onto the observers' own bodies, as the section turns from “no one saw” to the eyes given to the speaker.
Allah will show signs in the horizons and in themselves until truth becomes clear, then asks whether the Lord's witnessing of everything suffices.
بَصَآئِرُ have come from the Lord: whoever sees benefits himself and whoever is blind harms himself; the Prophet also denies being their keeper, distinguishing guidance from forced surveillance.
Hearing, eyes, and hearts avail a people nothing because they reject Allah's signs; the given faculties and denied ءَايَٰت are brought together exactly.
The One who originated people made hearing, eyes, and hearts for them; it directly parallels the reminder “Did We not make him two eyes?”
People leave their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and receive hearing, sight, and hearts, joining divine provision of perception to acquired knowledge.
Allah originates hearing, eyes, and hearts for people, another direct reminder that the faculty by which they judge visibility is itself given.
After shaping the human and breathing spirit into him, Allah makes hearing, eyes, and hearts; bodily form and perceptive gifts share one Creator.
The human is created from a mixed drop for testing and made hearing and seeing, so perception is both gift and part of accountability.
Hearing, sight, and heart are each subject to questioning, making the bestowed eye accountable rather than merely possessed.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا هِيَهْ repeats 90:12's disclosure question, but here the unknown destination belongs to the person whose scales are light.
نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ answers 101:10 with scorching fire, while the same question in surah 90 answers with liberating and feeding.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْحُطَمَةُ repeats the formula that tells the addressee what unaided sight cannot discover.
نَارُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْمُوقَدَةُ answers the disclosure question with Allah's kindled fire, the explicit reversal of 90:12-16's humane answer.
إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ makes that fire closed over them, exactly echoing surah 90's own closing fire after the sign-denier's failed supposition.
سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ places the wealthy sign-denier into Saqar immediately before another “what will make you know?” question.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا سَقَرُ is a third direct case where the section's formula opens onto fire.
لَوَّاحَةٌ لِّلْبَشَرِ describes Saqar as scorching or visibly altering human skin, fitting the bodily witness and watched human of this image.
عَلَيْهَا تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ places nineteen over the Fire, adding appointed overseers to the fire disclosed by 74:27.
The keepers of the Fire are angels and their number is a trial that exposes belief and doubt; divine knowledge fixes what human speculation cannot.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا سِجِّينٌ uses the disclosure formula for the destination of the wicked record.
كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ answers with an inscribed record, linking God-given knowledge to the permanent recording of supposedly unseen acts.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا عِلِّيُّونَ repeats the formula for the righteous record's high repository.
كِتَٰبٌ مَّرْقُومٌ again makes the answer a written record.
يَشْهَدُهُ ٱلْمُقَرَّبُونَ says those brought near witness that record, completing writing with present witnesses.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلطَّارِقُ asks for divinely given knowledge of the night visitor, preparing the visible answer and the guardian over every soul.
ٱلنَّجْمُ ٱلثَّاقِبُ answers with the piercing star, a remote visible marker like the section's sign seen from afar.
True righteousness includes giving loved wealth to orphans and the needy and spending فِى ٱلرِّقَابِ; feeding need and freeing necks meet in the same ethical program as the pass.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving the food, closely matching the concrete acts by which 90:12 explains the pass.
They feed solely for Allah's face, seeking neither reward nor thanks; the act's unseen intention is known to the divine watcher.
The left-handed person's account includes his failure to urge feeding the needy, connecting his “I did not know my account” in 69:26 to the food side of surah 90's answer.
The people of Saqar confess that they did not feed the needy, directly joining the fire disclosed in 74:27 to neglect of the act disclosed in 90:14-16.
Immediately before the Lord-at-the-watch-post image of 89:14 gives way to judgment of wealth, people are charged with not urging one another to feed the needy.
The denier does not urge feeding the needy, the precise social failure opposed by the pass's feeding scene.
The expiation for accidental killing includes تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُّؤْمِنَةٍ, a direct Quranic occurrence of freeing a neck.
The expiation for a broken oath includes تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, repeating the section's concrete act in another legal setting.
Obligatory alms have a share وَفِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, institutionalizing release from bondage alongside aid to the poor and needy.
The expiation for returning from ẓihār begins with تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ, another direct freeing of a neck.
Eyes do not encompass Allah while He encompasses all vision; the gaze is radically asymmetric, so failure to see the watcher gives no ground for thinking oneself unseen.
People have eyes with which they do not see and ears with which they do not hear; possession of the gift is reversed into culpable nonuse.
The ayah says eyes are not what go blind, but hearts within breasts; it sets a boundary between sensory sight and the perception needed to understand the pass.
Thamud are guided but prefer blindness to guidance, making chosen moral blindness the contrary of using the bestowed eye to take the shown road.
Allah could obliterate their eyes as they race for the path, leaving them unable to see; eye and road are joined by the withdrawal of the gift.
Their eyes were under a covering from Allah's reminder and they could not hear, combining veiled sight with refusal of the signs.
Believers do not fall upon their Lord's signs deaf and blind; their reception reverses the unused eyes and denied signs in this section.
The guilty finally say “we have seen and heard” and ask to return, but perception arrives after the arena of responsible action has closed.
“How well they will hear and see” on the day they come to Allah contrasts their present manifest error with unavoidable later perception.
فَضَرْبَ ٱلرِّقَابِ stages striking necks in battle, then binding and eventual release or ransom; it is the violent boundary against which “freeing a neck” is heard.
Charity done رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ seeks human eyes and is nullified; it reverses the deed done under God's sight without dependence on being seen by people.
Those who spend to be seen by people orient the act toward created observers, the opposite error to thinking no divine observer sees it.
The worshippers يُرَآءُونَ, performing for others' gaze; this corrupt visible display sits beside their refusal of small aid in 107:7.
The question asks who besides Allah could restore hearing and sight if He took them, reinforcing that the organs invoked by 90:8 remain wholly His gift.
The addressee must admit that Allah controls hearing and sight, moving from possession of eyes to dependence on their provider.
أَبْصِرْ بِهِۦ وَأَسْمِعْ praises Allah's perfect seeing and hearing and denies creatures any protecting partner, joining perception and guardianship.
The heart does not falsify what it saw, linking inward apprehension to the trustworthy vision later bounded in 53:17.
When visibly illuminating signs come, the people call them manifest magic; perceptibility does not prevent the sign-denier from covering what should be seen.
The she-camel is given as a visible sign, yet her people wrong her; a plainly shown ءَايَة can still be rejected.
The ruined settlement contains signs for those who read marks and lies on an enduring road, bringing visible signs and a travelled way together.
A clear sign is left from the destroyed town for people who reason, an enduring visible trace that must be interpreted rather than merely looked at.
Hiddenly needy people are recognized by their سِيمَا rather than importunate asking; a visible mark guides the observer toward the feeding obligation.
The guilty are recognized by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet, making the visible person an identified target at judgment.
Hypocrites could be recognized by their marks and are known through the tone of speech, while Allah knows all deeds; appearance, hearing, and divine knowledge overlap.
فَإِنْ ءَانَسْتُم مِّنْهُمْ رُشْدًا uses the section's ء ن س family for perceiving maturity, extending sensory noticing into responsible discernment.
وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا۟ forbids spying, setting a moral boundary around the human “eye” that gathers news even while divine observation remains unrestricted.
Solomon inspects the birds and notices the hoopoe's absence, beginning a scene of a ruler's watch and a scout who gathers distant news.
The absent bird must bring a clear authorization or face punishment, sharpening the accountable relation between scout and watcher.
The hoopoe returns with certain news from Sheba that Solomon did not encompass, exemplifying the news-gathering “eye” and the limits of a ruler's knowledge.
“Sit in wait for them at every مَرْصَدٍ” supplies a human ambush or observation station, a hostile counterpart to the lookout developed from the section's roots.
Shuayb says وَٱرْتَقِبُوٓا۟ إِنِّى مَعَكُمْ رَقِيبٌ, using the ر ق ب family for mutual waiting and watching as judgment approaches.
Moses spends the morning in the city خَآئِفًا يَتَرَقَّبُ, watchfully awaiting danger; the watcher here is a vulnerable fugitive.
Moses leaves the city fearful and يَتَرَقَّبُ, continuing the root's sense of alert waiting while himself exposed to pursuit.
فَٱرْتَقِبْ asks the Prophet to watch for the day the sky brings visible smoke, joining expectant watching to a sign appearing overhead.
فَٱرْتَقِبْ إِنَّهُم مُّرْتَقِبُونَ sets the Prophet's waiting against the opponents' waiting, a reciprocal use of the section's watcher-root.
فَٱرْتَقِبْهُمْ وَٱصْطَبِرْ commands Salih to watch his people during the she-camel test, making observation part of waiting for their response to a sign.
Successive agents before and behind a person guard him by Allah's command, a mobile version of the protective watcher.
Allah sends guardians over people until death and His messengers take the soul without neglect, extending observation into custody.
وَشَاهِدٍ وَمَشْهُودٍ pairs watcher and watched as an oath, distilling the relation around which this section is built.
The persecutors sit as witnesses to what they do to believers, a grim human watching scene itself enclosed by Allah's witness in 85:9.
وَٱللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَىْءٍ شَهِيدٌ places the watchers of 85:7 under the universal divine witness.
Some hypocrites are unknown to the Prophet but known to Allah, drawing a boundary between human recognition and the observer who misses no concealed person.
Concealed charity to the poor is better, and Allah is fully aware of the act; invisibility to people preserves rather than erases the deed.
The show-offs of 107:6 withhold even small aid, joining corrupted concern for human sight to failure of the mercy enacted by the pass.
The person whose scales are light supplies the judged subject of the disclosure question in 101:10.
His destination is a hāwiyah, the still-unknown reality that 101:10 asks about and 101:11 identifies as blazing fire.
The target of the Crusher gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, closely resembling the wealth-boaster whose claim in surah 90 is made under an unacknowledged gaze.
He supposes his wealth makes him immortal, another wealth-based supposition exposed by the coming fire and divine account.
The wealth-counter will be cast into the Crusher, setting the event that 104:5 asks the addressee to have disclosed.
The solitary man of the passage is given extensive wealth, linking the later fire question to a figure who treats provision as grounds for resistance.
He stubbornly opposes Allah's signs, identifying the fire-bound figure as the same kind of sign-denier named at the end of surah 90.
سَأُرْهِقُهُۥ صَعُودًا promises him a punishing ascent, a dark counterpart to the difficult pass whose ascent consists in freeing and feeding.
The wicked person's record is in Sijjin, supplying the object about which 83:8 asks and 83:9 answers “an inscribed book.”
The righteous person's record is in Illiyyin, supplying the counterpart about which 83:19 asks and 83:20 answers.
The oath by heaven and the night visitor begins a sequence whose distant piercing sign leads to the guardian over every soul.
فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ مِمَّ خُلِقَ turns the guarded human of 86:4 into an observer commanded to inspect his own creation.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْحَآقَّةُ uses divine disclosure for the reality of judgment in the same surah where the left-handed person later says he did not know his account.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلدِّينِ asks for disclosure of the day on which the guardians' records become account.
The question “what will make you know the Day of Judgment?” is repeated, stressing human inability to see that reality unaided.
No soul controls anything for another and command belongs to Allah, answering the repeated question with the boundary of human power.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا يَوْمُ ٱلْفَصْلِ uses the same God-given-knowledge formula for the decisive day when hidden responsibility is separated out.
وَمَآ أَدْرَىٰكَ مَا ٱلْقَارِعَةُ begins the surah's first disclosure, before the second question narrows from the event to the blazing fate of light scales.
Good sent ahead is found with Allah and He sees what people do; even quiet expenditure is preserved before the observer.
Allah forms people in wombs however He wills, bringing the human image itself under the knowledge of the One from whom nothing is hidden in 3:5.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, showing hidden divine action around people plotting to withhold provision.
The garden owners whisper that no needy person should enter that day, a concealed refusal of feeding that the surrounding divine visitation exposes.
Aaron asks why Moses did not تَرْقُبْ قَوْلِى; the root has the secondary sense of heeding or guarding a word, plausibly extending watching from persons to entrusted speech.
The rhetorical question asks whether they do not know that Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose, directly correcting imagined secrecy.
Whether people reveal what is within themselves or hide it, Allah calls them to account for it; hidden inward material becomes an explicit reckoning.
The addressee is warned that Allah knows whatever is concealed within breasts or disclosed, extending observation behind outward appearance.
The question asks whether they know that Allah knows their secret and private counsel, another pointed exposure of speech thought to lack a listener.
Allah knows what people conceal and what they reveal, closing the divide on which an unwatched deed depends.
Even if speech is voiced aloud, Allah knows the secret and what is still more hidden, placing divine hearing beyond sensory access.
Allah knows spoken words and what people conceal, a direct counterpart to the watched utterance in 50:18.
The Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they disclose, making inward intention and outward act equally visible to knowledge.
The Lord knows what breasts conceal and what people disclose, repeated in a judgment context where He chooses and decides.
Not an atom in heavens or earth is absent from Allah, and nothing smaller or greater escapes a clear record; this joins minute observation to writing.
Allah knows heaven and earth, concealed and disclosed acts, and what breasts contain, gathering all levels of hiddenness under one knowledge.
Allah hears the woman who argues concerning her husband and her dialogue with the Prophet; a private human complaint is already heard and seen.
Allah has enumerated deeds that people forgot and is witness over everything, showing that human forgetting does not erase observed action.
Allah writes what people send ahead and the traces they leave, having enumerated everything in a clear register.
Allah's book speaks truth against them because their deeds were being copied, turning ongoing observation into documentary testimony.
Everything people did is in written records, directly denying that any deed passed without preservation.
Every small and great thing is inscribed, completing 54:52's record with the same exhaustive scale as the observing eye.
Everything has been counted in a book, so the eventual account rests on a complete record rather than recalled appearances.
The human will be told what he sent ahead and left behind, making unseen consequences part of the disclosed account.
Every soul will know what it has brought, the moment recorded action becomes self-knowledge.
Allah taught the human what he did not know, closely matching the section's claim that the pass must be made known by God.
The human transgresses, identifying the conduct whose supposedly unwatched instance culminates in 96:14's question about Allah seeing.
The human transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient; his mistaken self-sight is answered by Allah's sight in 96:14.
“Have you seen the one who forbids?” turns the audience's gaze toward the offender whom 96:14 places under Allah's gaze.
The offender stops a servant while he prays, supplying the specific visible act judged by 96:14.
Allah will summon the guards of Hell against the defiant offender, filling the scene around the watched man with appointed enforcers.
Whoever turns from Allah's reminder is raised blind, making lost sight the consequence of refusing guidance.
The raised person asks why he is blind although he once saw, explicitly confronting the difference between possessing sight and using it rightly.
Allah answers that His signs came and were forgotten, so the sign-denier is now left forgotten; rejected ءَايَٰت explain the blindness.
They suppose no trial will come, become blind and deaf, and after reprieve many do so again, while Allah sees what they do.
The people of the blaze admit that listening or reasoning would have kept them from the Fire, exposing their failure to use the faculties given in 67:23.
The guilty see the Fire, know they are falling into it, and find no escape, another final sight of what earlier remained beyond their view.
When the promised punishment is seen near, the deniers' faces darken and they are told this is what they demanded, turning denied warning into immediate sight.
Only when people see Allah's might do they profess belief and reject their former partners; perception arrives after their prior signs were denied.
Belief no longer benefits once divine might is seen, establishing the temporal boundary between responsible trust and compelled sight.
The adorned heaven is protected from every rebellious devil, supplying the guarding action that 37:8-10 continues with attempted eavesdropping.
Allah places constellations in heaven and beautifies them for observers, providing the visible high scene that 15:17 immediately guards.
The ruined place lies on an enduring road; this ayah, rather than 15:75 alone, supplies the roadway on which its signs remain visible.
The sky is made a guarded canopy while people turn away from its signs, bringing protective watch and neglected ءَايَٰت together.
The harmful mosque is built as an إِرْصَادًا, an outpost for an enemy of Allah and His messenger, giving the lookout image a covert human use.
The human is asked what deluded him concerning his generous Lord, opening the creation-to-guardians sequence with a false confidence like 90:7's.
The Lord created, proportioned, and balanced the human, identifying the maker whose knowledge precedes the observing guardians in 82:10.
Allah assembled the human in whatever form He willed, a direct Quranic counterpart to the section's attention to the human image.
The dwellings of ʿAd and Thamud are visibly evident, yet Satan barred them from the way although they had insight; visible remains, perception, and a blocked path converge.
The expelled people thought their fortresses would protect them, but Allah reached them from where they did not expect and tells possessors of sight to take heed.
The deniers almost strike the Prophet with their eyes when they hear the reminder, making the gaze itself a hostile means of targeting a visible person.
The Fire has stern angelic keepers who never disobey Allah, another direct meeting of fire with vigilant guardians.
Owners are commanded to grant emancipation contracts to those in bondage and give them from Allah's wealth, concretely extending the freeing-neck side of the pass.
The wealth passage following the Lord's watch post charges people with failing to honor the orphan, matching the orphan named in surah 90's feeding scene.
The judgment-denier repels the orphan, supplying the first concrete failure before 107:3's refusal to urge feeding the needy.
The one who is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient closely matches the wealth-secure human whose supposition of independence the section exposes.
He denies the best promise, joining withheld wealth to denial of what divine disclosure presents as true.
Allah eases him toward hardship, a grim counter-direction to the humane ascent through the pass.
His wealth does not avail when he falls, answering the boastful reliance on accumulated wealth.
The believing speaker entrusts his affair to Allah because Allah sees the servants, making divine sight the ground of protection amid a hostile plot.
Believing men are commanded to lower their gaze, and Allah is fully aware of what they do; the bestowed eye itself falls under moral observation.
Believing women are likewise commanded to lower their gaze and guard themselves, marking an ethical boundary on human looking.
Those with diseased hearts suppose Allah will not expose their rancor, another false supposition that concealed inward reality can escape disclosure.
Allah formed people and made their forms good, plausibly extending the section's small human image to the divine fashioning of every bodily form.
Allah formed people and perfected their forms, then states that the final return is to Him; visible form and return to its maker are joined.
The command not to enter others' houses until seeking recognition or permission sets a privacy boundary on the human impulse to observe what is inside.
Jacob commands his sons to seek news of Joseph and his brother, a family search for hidden persons that resembles the section's news-gathering eye.
Pharaoh's wife calls the found infant a comfort of the eye and prevents his killing, adding human protection to the Moses-under-the-divine-eye sequence.
When the husband sees the shirt torn from behind, the material trace exposes what occurred without an eyewitness, a concrete sign disclosing a concealed act.
The Prophet denies possessing the unseen and asks whether the blind and seeing are equal, distinguishing revelation-dependent knowledge from ordinary sight.
The two parties are likened to blind and deaf versus seeing and hearing, making responsible perception a moral distinction rather than mere possession of organs.
A group conceals within themselves what they do not show the Prophet, and Allah states that He knows what they hide.
They consume inherited wealth greedily, continuing the watched community's misuse of provision after neglecting orphan and needy.
They love wealth with consuming love, supplying the motive behind the failures that the following surah's pass reverses.
